extraReferences.title: Digging with 'hands': observations of food capture in the flying gurnard Dactylopterus volitans (Linnaeus, 1758). Journal of Natural History 53: 2489–2501
Biologia reprodutiva do falso-voador, Dactylopterus volitans (Teleostei: Dactylopteridae), no litoral norte do Estado de São Paulo, Brasil. Arquivos de Ciências do Mar 35: 125–129
extraReferences.authors: Machado J.F., Zambeli R.M., Vianna M.

anatomy.lede: Folded up, a flying gurnard is a heavy-scaled bottom fish with big eyes. Its secret is in the pectoral fins, which work as shovels and as a sudden pair of wings.

hotspots.label: Large eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are large, and the body colour is very variable: brown or greenish with reddish or yellowish patches.

hotspots.label: Front of the pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The front part of each pectoral fin is used to explore the seabed and to dig. Its stiff, unsegmented leading ray forms a digging edge.

hotspots.label: Folded 'wing'
hotspots.text: The back part of the pectoral fin, folded here, opens into a huge semi-transparent fan with bright blue tips when the fish is excited.

hotspots.label: Pelvic fin
hotspots.text: Flying gurnards have been seen 'walking' over sand on their pelvic fins while searching for food.

hotspots.label: Armoured scales
hotspots.text: The body is covered in heavy, protective scales.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: Adults can reach about 50 cm and 1.8 kg, though about 38 cm is more usual.

body.lede: Each pectoral fin is really two tools in one, and the whole fish is wrapped in armour.

systems.title: A fin with two halves
systems.text: Each pectoral fin has a digging part, with flexible segmented rays behind a stiff front ray, and a larger rear part supported by unsegmented rays that forms the 'wing'.

systems.title: Digging, then sucking
systems.text: Once the fin has uncovered prey, the fish catches it by suction, drawing it into the mouth with a rush of water.

systems.title: Colour on demand
systems.text: It can shift from very dark brown or grey to almost white depending on the ground beneath it and other conditions.

mind.lede: Close watching of how the flying gurnard feeds has shown a careful, repeated digging routine.

studies.title: Digging with 'hands'
studies.text: Usually only one pectoral fin digs at a time. It sweeps forward and inwards, twists and presses down so the stiff front ray bites into the sediment, then pulls back and out to stir it up.

studies.title: Short bursts
studies.text: Each dig lasts from one to seven strokes, made at between about one and four strokes a second.

survival.lede: A slow walker on open sand, the flying gurnard relies on armour and a surprise.

tactics.title: The sudden flash
tactics.text: Spreading the brightly coloured pectoral fins may startle a predator long enough for the fish to escape.

tactics.title: Armour
tactics.text: Heavy, protective scales cover the body.

threats.title: Caught with shrimp
threats.text: Off south-eastern Brazil, many flying gurnards are taken as bycatch by shrimp trawlers. Most of the catch are juveniles, and the shrimp closed season does not protect the spawning fish.

threats.title: Fished and kept
threats.text: It is also of minor commercial importance, caught as a gamefish, and sold for aquariums.

life.lede: Flying gurnards begin life adrift in open water and settle to the seabed only later.

stages.name: Floating larva
stages.text: Many species of flying gurnard have an extended larval stage that floats freely in the ocean, while the adults live on the bottom.

stages.name: Growing up
stages.text: In one study of 592 fish caught off Brazil, lengths ranged from about 7 to 35.5 cm, and fish of around 10 cm were the most common.

stages.name: Maturity
stages.text: Half of females were mature at 17.4 cm and half of males at 19.3 cm.

stages.name: Spawning
stages.text: Off Brazil, the ovaries and testes grew heavier between November and February, which points to that being the spawning season.
